records.place: Vilanoviña, Meis, Val do Salnés, Rías Baixas, Galicia

wine.name: Pazo Señorans Selección de Añada
wine.grapes: Albariño alone, as a wine labelled Rías Baixas Albariño must be.
wine.sites: Os Bancales, a single plot of old Albariño on the slope behind the sixteenth century pazo at Vilanoviña, in Meis, on granite; the vines average more than forty five years by the house's sheet.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel with no malolactic fermentation, the wine then rests on its lees in steel tanks for more than thirty months, as the house's sheet gives, and sees no oak at any stage. It spends at least a year more in bottle before it is released.
wine.glass: Pale straw with green glints; white peach, ripe lemon and bay leaf over sea salt, with a broad, dense body built by the long lees, bright acidity and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Ready when it is released, several years after the harvest; the house's own sheet gives it five years more at its peak, and it can hold for a decade.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, a little warmer than a young Albariño; it needs no decanter, though it opens in a wide white wine glass.

label.means: A selection of one vintage, held for years on its lees before release; a dry wine, never a late harvest.
The Denominación de Origen of the Galician coast, ratified in 1988; Meis lies in its Val do Salnés subzone.
Under the Rías Baixas rules a wine named for the grape is Albariño alone.

records.table: Pazo de Señorans holds its Selección de Añada on the lees in steel for thirty months and more, then a year in bottle, never in oak, so this Albariño from Meis comes to the table broad and saline, and it shows how well the grape can age.
records.story: The house takes its name from a pazo, a Galician manor house, that it dates to the sixteenth century, at Vilanoviña in the parish of Meis, in the Val do Salnés. On 11 October 1980 the Spanish government recognised the Denominación Específica Albariño. Because the law of the day would not let a denomination carry the name of a grape, the regulating council recalls, it was ratified as the Denominación de Origen Rías Baixas in July 1988, with Val do Salnés among its first three subzones. The family that held the pazo began making wine there in 1989, and the estate also has its own distillery for orujo, the spirit of the pressed skins. Where Albariño is mostly bottled young, the family set aside the fruit of a single plot of old vines behind the house and kept its wine in steel on its lees for more than thirty months, then a year in bottle, to show that the grape could age: that wine is Selección de Añada. Pour it for a guest who thinks of Albariño as a summer white. It is the grape given years, broader and saltier, and it belongs beside turbot or scallops rather than with an aperitif.

others.name: Pazo Señorans Albariño
others.note: The house's young wine, bottled each year from the estate's Albariño of the Val do Salnés.

others.name: Pazo Señorans Aguardiente de Orujo
others.note: A spirit distilled from the pressed skins in the estate's own distillery.

traps: Selección de Añada is a dry Albariño held for years on its lees, never a late harvest or a sweet wine.
Its long ageing is in steel tanks, not in oak barrels: the breadth comes from the lees, not from wood.
Pazo is Galician for a country manor house; on a label it names the house, not a style or a rank.

cards.front: Pazo de Señorans Selección de Añada: how long on its lees, and in what?
cards.back: More than thirty months in stainless steel tanks, with no oak, and then at least a year in bottle.

cards.front: Pazo de Señorans: what is the house named for?
cards.back: A pazo, a Galician manor house of the sixteenth century, at Vilanoviña in the parish of Meis.

questions.q: A guest asks what gives Pazo de Señorans Selección de Añada its breadth, since it sees no oak. Which answer is right?
opts: More than thirty months on its lees in steel
A year of ageing in new French oak barrels
Grapes left late on the vine to shrivel
A share of Treixadura from Condado do Tea
questions.exp: The house keeps it on its lees in stainless steel for over thirty months, then a year in bottle; it never sees a barrel, and it is Albariño alone, picked for a dry wine.

questions.q: In which year did the family begin making wine at Pazo de Señorans, in Meis?
questions.exp: Wine was first made at the pazo in 1989, the year after Rías Baixas became a Denominación de Origen; 1980 is the year of the Denominación Específica Albariño, 1928 of Fefiñanes's brand and 1973 of Do Ferreiro's first wine.

report: The house's own shop sheet gives the steel, the more than thirty months on the lees, no malolactic and the five year window; its guided visit sheet dates the manor house to the sixteenth century and names the distillery; the Consejo Regulador's history gives 11 October 1980, July 1988 and the three first subzones, and why the name Albariño gave way.

The single plot behind the pazo and the year in bottle rest on European Cellars and the Wine Scholar Guild guide (a Spanish merchant, Vinos Cutanda, gives the same); the plot's name, Los Bancales, is printed by the importer alone and is left out.

Left out for want of a second citable source: the purchase of the pazo in 1979 (European Cellars, beside a writer's own site that cannot be cited), the first vintage of Selección de Añada as 1995 (one tasting note), the tale that it began with a tank forgotten for a vintage (the importer alone), and any claim that it is made only in some years.
The library's founded year, 1989, is kept and agrees with a winery tourism page that dates the family's winemaking to that year.

Living names met and kept out: the founding couple, one of whom (Marisol Bueno) is in people.json; her husband, Javier Mareque, is not, his status not settled, for the read-together agent to list as a precaution.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, two restricted to the house's domain and one to its importers', with two more shared with the group on the Consejo Regulador's own domain.

changed: wine.sites: the plot is now named, Os Bancales, as the house's own shop sheet for Selección de Añada names it (with its vines of more than forty five years); the author had left the name out as the importer's alone, but the house prints it, a primary source for its own vineyard.
open: The first vintage of Selección de Añada is given as 1995 by two Spanish merchants' pages, not by the house; it stays out.

The house's sheet gives the steel, the more than thirty months on the lees, no malolactic and a five year window, but not the year in bottle, which rests on the importer and the Wine Scholar Guild guide; it stands as theirs.

The year the pazo was bought, 1979, appears in the importer's account and a writer's own site that cannot be cited; it stays out, and one listing dates the building to the fourteenth century against the house's sixteenth.

records.place: Plaza de Fefiñanes, Cambados, Val do Salnés, Rías Baixas, Galicia

wine.name: Albariño de Fefiñanes
wine.grapes: Albariño alone, from Cambados in the Val do Salnés.
wine.sites: Albariño from vineyards around Cambados, on the Arousa inlet in the Val do Salnés, brought to the cellar inside the palace on the town square.
wine.making: Fermented at a low temperature in stainless steel vats, with no oak, as the house's own sheet gives, and bottled before the middle of the year after the harvest, to be sold and drunk young.
wine.glass: Lemon pith, green apple and acacia blossom over crushed shell and a touch of bay; light in body, with bright, crisp acidity and a clean, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk young, in the year or two after bottling; for an Albariño of Fefiñanes with more time behind it, the house makes its III Año.
wine.serve: About 10 degrees Celsius, as the house's sheet advises; straight from the bottle with no decanter, into a medium white wine glass.

label.means: The brand the house created and registered in 1928, with a label drawn that year.
The cellar inside the palace of the viscounts of Fefiñanes, on the square of Cambados.
The Galician Denominación de Origen of 1988; Cambados lies in its Val do Salnés subzone.

records.table: From a cellar inside the old palace of the viscounts of Fefiñanes, on the square of Cambados, comes Albariño de Fefiñanes, a brand registered in 1928; fermented cool in steel and bottled young, it is lemon pith, apple and salt beside oysters.
records.story: The palace of Fefiñanes stands on the square of Cambados, by the Arousa inlet. Its building, begun by one family in the sixteenth century, was carried on, as the house tells it, by a son of the estate born there in 1583 who served the king and became the first Viscount of Fefiñanes, and it was finished in the seventeenth century. Wine has been made in the palace since that century, by the house's account, and in the first years of the twentieth its cellar became a business. In 1928 the house created and registered the brand Albariño de Fefiñanes and released its first vintage under it, with a label drawn that year by a jeweller and jet carver of Santiago de Compostela; it was one of the first white wines of the region to carry a commercial label. In 1929, the house recalls, the wine won an award at the international exhibition in Barcelona. When Rías Baixas was ratified as a Denominación de Origen in 1988, Cambados fell within its Val do Salnés subzone, and in 1995 the house first made a barrel fermented Albariño named for the viscount's birth year, 1583. Albariño de Fefiñanes stays the plain one: steel, no oak, bottled young, the Salnés at its simplest, under a name and a label of 1928.

others.name: 1583 Albariño de Fefiñanes
others.note: Fermented in used Bordeaux barrels of French oak and briefly on its lees, first made in 1995.

others.name: Albariño de Fefiñanes III Año
others.note: Fermented in steel, then held long in tank, part of that time on its lees, and sold in its third year.

traps: The figure 1583 is the birth year of the first Viscount of Fefiñanes, not a vintage and not the date of the palace.
III Año means the wine is sold in its third year after long ageing in tank, not that it spent three years in bottle.
The plain Albariño de Fefiñanes sees no oak; the barrels belong to 1583 Albariño de Fefiñanes.

cards.front: Albariño de Fefiñanes: what happened to the brand and its label in 1928?
cards.back: The house created and registered the brand, a Santiago jeweller and jet carver drew the label, and the first vintage was released under it.

cards.front: What does the figure 1583 on a Fefiñanes label stand for?
cards.back: The birth year of the first Viscount of Fefiñanes; it names the house's barrel fermented Albariño.

questions.q: A guest wants to know how the plain Albariño de Fefiñanes is made. Which description fits?
opts: Fermented cool in steel and bottled young
Fermented in French oak with stirred lees
Held thirty months in tank before release
Blended with Treixadura from Condado do Tea
questions.exp: The house ferments it at a low temperature in stainless steel and bottles it before the middle of the next year; the barrels are for 1583 and the long tank ageing for III Año.

questions.q: In which year did the Fefiñanes cellar create and register its brand, Albariño de Fefiñanes?
questions.exp: The brand, its label and its first vintage all date from 1928; 1929 is the year of its Barcelona award, 1988 of the Denominación de Origen and 1583 of the first viscount's birth.

report: The house's own pages and sheets give the wine since the seventeenth century, the cellar as a business in the first years of the twentieth, the brand and label of 1928 with the Santiago jeweller and jet carver, the first vintage of 1928, the Barcelona award of 1929, the steel, the bottling in the first half of the next year, the 10 degree serve, the 1583 cuvée's first vintage of 1995 and its barrels, and III Año's long tank ageing.

The library's p-fefinanes is wrong on 1583: it says the wine is named for the palace's date and its trap says 1583 refers to the palace, but the house's own page says 1583 is the year the first Viscount of Fefiñanes was born; this record follows the house.

founded is left empty: 1904, the plan's and the region record's year, was found with the US importer Kysela and was not confirmed by a second source read in this run (Spanish Wine Lover gives no founding year), while the house says only the first years of the twentieth century.

One of the first white wines of the region with a commercial label rests on Spanish Wine Lover and on Decanter, which calls it the first bodega to bottle a varietal Albariño, in 1928; the record keeps the softer claim of the two.

The palace's completion is given as 1621 (Spanish Wine Lover) and 1647 (Kysela), so the story says the seventeenth century; the name of the jeweller who drew the label is given by the house but his dates were not found, so he is described.

Left out, on one source each: the label unchanged since 1928, the bottle of Rhine shape and the Galician Mosel name of the 1950s, and the number of growers who sell the house their grapes; the living owner named by the importer is kept out.

Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 35, three restricted to the house's domain and two to merchants' and writers' pages. The first Viscount of Fefiñanes is the house's own name for the man born in 1583, a title and not a claim of rank, so the lint's note on it is answered.

open: founded stays empty: 1904 is given by the importer (Kysela) and a Spanish merchant (Vinissimus), with the two founders of the bodega, but the house's own pages say only the first years of the twentieth century; the integrator may set 1904 if a primary source is found.

The palace was begun in the sixteenth century by a lord of Fefiñanes who counselled Philip II and finished by his nephew, the first viscount, a title granted by Philip IV, on the town's own tourism page alone; the record keeps the house's telling, which agrees.

records.place: Cambados, Val do Salnés, Rías Baixas, Galicia

wine.name: Martín Códax Albariño
wine.sites: Small plots worked by the member growers in the heart of the Val do Salnés, the cool, coastal subzone around Cambados.
wine.making: The growers pick by hand, and the grapes come in from their plots in the heart of the Val do Salnés. After fermentation the wine is kept for a time on its lees, which the house says balances the aromas of the lees with the grape's own, and it is bottled young.
wine.glass: Lemon, pink grapefruit and white peach with a touch of rose petal; light and bright, with brisk acidity and a clean, faintly salty finish.
wine.ageing: Made for youth: drink it within a year or two of the harvest, while the fruit and the sea air in it are at their brightest.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanter; a standard white wine glass, with shellfish, grilled fish or tapas.

label.means: A Galician jongleur of the thirteenth century whose seven love songs of the Vigo sea survive, six with their music.
Named for its grape, the wine is Albariño alone under the Rías Baixas rules.
The Denominación de Origen of Galicia's southern coast, ratified in July 1988.

records.table: Martín Códax is the Cambados winery founded in 1985 by fifty growers of the Val do Salnés and named for a medieval Galician troubadour; its Albariño is bright, lemony and lightly salty, made to pour young with shellfish.
records.story: Martín Códax was a jongleur of the thirteenth century, thought to have come from Vigo, whose seven cantigas de amigo give voice to a girl waiting by the sea of Vigo for a lover who has gone. The songs survive with their music, six of the seven notated, on a single parchment that a Madrid antiquarian bookseller found in the early twentieth century, and it is held in the Morgan Library in New York. In 1985, by the house's history, fifty growers of the Val do Salnés joined their grapes and their capital to build a winery at Cambados. Its first Albariño, which carried the poet's name, followed in 1986, from plots in the heart of the Salnés. Two years later, in July 1988, Rías Baixas was ratified as a Denominación de Origen, grown out of the Denominación Específica Albariño of 1980, and the growers' winery grew with it. Its later labels keep the poet close: Vindel is named for the parchment that holds his songs. Pour Martín Códax Albariño as the grape's young, bright face, and tell the guest that the name on the label is that of a medieval singer of the sea.

others.name: Martín Códax Lías
others.note: Albariño stirred on its fine lees for six to seven months, then held up to a year in tank before bottling.

others.name: Martín Códax Vindel
others.note: An Albariño named for the parchment that holds the poet's seven songs.

traps: Martín Códax is a growers' winery at Cambados, not one family's estate, and the name on the label is a medieval poet's, not a founder's.
Martín Códax Albariño is Albariño alone; a wine labelled with the Val do Salnés subzone may hold other approved grapes for up to three tenths.

cards.front: Who was Martín Códax, whose name the Cambados winery took?
cards.back: A Galician jongleur of the thirteenth century, whose seven love songs of the Vigo sea survive with music for six of them.

cards.front: Martín Códax: when was the winery founded, and by whom?
cards.back: In 1985, by fifty growers of the Val do Salnés who pooled their grapes and their capital.

questions.q: A guest asks which grapes are in Martín Códax Albariño. What do you answer?
opts: Albariño alone
Albariño with Loureira and Caíño Blanco
Albariño with Treixadura
Godello with a little Albariño
questions.exp: A Rías Baixas wine named for Albariño must be that grape alone; Loureira and Caíño Blanco belong to O Rosal blends, and Treixadura to those of Condado do Tea.

questions.q: The seven songs of Martín Códax survive with their music on one parchment. Where is it held?
opts: The Morgan Library in New York
The cathedral archive of Santiago
The town hall of Cambados
The monastery of Armenteira
questions.exp: The parchment, found by a Madrid bookseller in the early twentieth century and notated for six of the songs, is held in the Morgan Library in New York, far from the coast it sings of.

report: The plan's why and the region record both found the house in 1986 as a cooperative; the house's own history gives 1985 and fifty growers, as do Decanter China and Cellar Tours, and gives 1986 as the year its Albariño was created, so founded is 1985 and the story tells both years.
The house's legal form is not settled here: two accounts call it a cooperative, the house says a group of growers, so the record says a growers' winery and never cooperative.

The making is thin on purpose: the house's page gives hand picking by its growers, plots in the heart of the Val do Salnés and time on the lees, but no source read gives the vessels or the length on the lees for this wine, so neither is given (stainless steel rests on one secondary account).

The parchment's year of discovery is given as 1913 and 1914 and the bookseller's dates were not read, so he is described; the songs' texts also survive in two songbooks without music, which is why the record says they survive with their music on one parchment rather than only there.

Lías: the house's shop page gives six months of stirring on fine lees and a year more in tank; its launch year, 2005, rests on Decanter China alone and is left out. The membership counts (270 partners, about 300 families) are volatile and left out.
Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35, two restricted to the house's domain, and one shared with Terras Gauda on the Rías Baixas promotion site, which gave nothing on either house's making.

changed: wine.label: the poet's seven love songs survived with their music; now six with their music, since the Morgan Library's parchment notates six and leaves the sixth song's staff empty (the Morgan facsimile, IMSLP, OMI).

story: in 1985 the growers built a winery at Cambados and named it for the poet; now the winery of 1985 and its first Albariño of 1986 carrying the poet's name, since one account gives the growers' first body as an association of Albariño growers of Vilariño and Cambados that took the name Bodegas Martín Códax only in 1998, while the house dates its Martín Códax Albariño to 1986.
others: Lías was stirred on its lees for six months and then held a year in tank; now six to seven months and then up to a year in tank, as the house's own Lías sheet gives.
open: The growers' first association and the change to a company named Bodegas Martín Códax in 1998 rest on one directory account and are not told.
The parchment's year of discovery (1913 or 1914) is unsettled, so the record says the early twentieth century; the Morgan acquired it in 1977, on one journal's account, and it is not told.

records.place: Lores, Meaño, Val do Salnés, Rías Baixas, Galicia

wine.name: Do Ferreiro Cepas Vellas
wine.grapes: Albariño alone, from very old vines.
wine.sites: One plot of Albariño in front of the family house at Lores, in Meaño, trained high on pergolas, its vines more than two hundred years old by the family's account.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts in stainless steel tanks, it is then raised for about a year on its fine lees before it is bottled, the span moving a little with the vintage.
wine.glass: Quince, ripe pear and lemon peel over sea salt and beeswax, with a dense, textured body, firm acidity and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and reserved in its first years, it rewards time in bottle; its importer gives it ten to twenty years in a good cellar.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, not colder; let a young bottle open in a carafe or in the glass; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: Galician for old vines: here one plot of very old Albariño, not a legal category.
Galician for the blacksmith's, the name the family gave its wine.
The Denominación de Origen of 1988; Meaño lies within its Val do Salnés subzone.

records.table: Do Ferreiro's Cepas Vellas comes from one plot of Albariño at Lores, in Meaño, whose pergola vines the family dates back more than two centuries; fermented with native yeasts and kept long on its lees, it is dense, salty and made to age.
records.story: Ferreiro is Galician for blacksmith, and Do Ferreiro, the blacksmith's, honours the family's old trade at the forge, as its importer tells it. At Lores, in Meaño in the Val do Salnés, the family grew Albariño, and in 1973 the founder began making wine at the family house. When Rías Baixas was ratified as a Denominación de Origen in 1988, the founder, by the same account, was among those who founded it, fourteen wineries in all by the regulating council's count. In front of the house grows the plot behind Cepas Vellas: Albariño that the family dates to the eighteenth century, its vines more than two hundred years old, trained high on pergolas so that the Atlantic wind can dry the bunches. Its grapes are kept apart from the family's younger vines, fermented with the native yeasts of the vineyard and given about a year on their fine lees, so that the wine gains texture and salt rather than perfume. The house holds to the pergola, the old way of the Salnés. Cepas Vellas answers the guest who believes Albariño must be drunk young: a single plot of very old vines, dense and saline, which repays years in the cellar.

others.name: Do Ferreiro Albariño
others.note: The estate wine, from the family's younger granite plots around Meaño and its neighbouring villages.

traps: Cepas Vellas means old vines; it names this plot's wine and is no legal category of Rías Baixas.
Albariño is trained high on pergolas here to fight the Atlantic damp, so that air moves under the canopy, not to raise the yield.
A list may print the company's name, which is the founder's own, rather than Do Ferreiro: it is the same Meaño house.

cards.front: Do Ferreiro Cepas Vellas: what does the name mean, and what does it describe?
cards.back: Galician for old vines: one plot in front of the family house at Lores, its vines more than two centuries old by the family's account.

cards.front: Do Ferreiro: how is the old vine Albariño fermented and raised?
cards.back: With native yeasts in stainless steel, then about a year on its fine lees before bottling.

questions.q: A guest asks how the vines behind Do Ferreiro Cepas Vellas are trained. What is the answer?
opts: High on pergolas, against the Atlantic damp
Low as free standing bush vines
On wires close to warm slate
Along terraces walled in schist
questions.exp: The old Albariño of Lores is trained high on pergolas so that the sea wind can dry the bunches; bush vines and slate or schist terraces belong to drier, warmer places.

questions.q: In 1973 a family of growers at Lores began making wine at its house. What does the name it gave its wine, Do Ferreiro, mean?
opts: The blacksmith's
The ferryman's
The iron gate
The old mill
questions.exp: Ferreiro is Galician for blacksmith, the family's old trade by its importer's account; the name has nothing to do with a ferry, a gate or a mill.

report: No page of the house's own was found (a search restricted to its domain returned nothing), so the record stands on its US importer, De Maison Selections, and on merchants; it carries no primary source.

The founding year 1973 rests on Bodeboca and De Maison; the library gives none. The native yeasts, steel and about eleven months on the lees rest on De Maison and Wine.com; the vines' age of more than two hundred years on De Maison, Bodeboca and Vinissimus.

The blacksmith father behind the name and the family's part in founding the Denominación in 1988 are each told by De Maison, with an unnamed second account of fourteen founding wineries; both are hedged as the importer's telling and a refuter should try them first.

The plot's planting year is given as 1785 and as before a document of 1790, so the story says the eighteenth century; the first separate bottling of Cepas Vellas (1995, one account) and of the first wine named Do Ferreiro (1986, or a decade after 1973) are left out.

The library's p-do-ferreiro prints the living founder's name in its producer field (Do Ferreiro (Gerardo Méndez)); the record never names him. Living names met and kept out: the founder (in people.json) and his son and daughter, Manuel (Manu) and Encarna Méndez, for the read-together agent.
A Meaño house of a related name, Bodegas y Viñedos Rodrigo Méndez, is a separate winery; it is not this one.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, one restricted to the house's domain with no result and one refused by the search tool for two blocked press domains.

changed: story: Do Ferreiro honoured the trade of the founder's father; now the family's old trade at the forge, since the importer's page says the family's blacksmith trade and a Spanish guide a family of blacksmiths, and neither names the father.

story: father and son were among the growers who founded the Denominación in 1988; now the founder alone, with the regulating council's own count of fourteen wineries in 1988, since no source read names the son among them.

wine.making, story and cards: about eleven months on the fine lees; now about a year, since the importer's sheet gives eleven months for a recent vintage, a merchant about twelve and a tasting of the 2007 a little over a year.
questions: the story question's explanation gives the blacksmith as the family's old trade, not the founder's father's.
sources: the Wine.com sheet gives way to the regulating council's own history of the Denominación, a primary source for the fourteen wineries of 1988; the record had none.
open: The house has no page of its own that the search tool reaches; the record stands on its importer, merchants and the regulating council. Two Spanish guides that confirm 1973, the blacksmiths and the fourteen founders carry the living founder's name in their addresses, so they are named in the review file only by publisher.
Cepas Vellas has been bottled on its own since the 1995 vintage, in the better years, by the importer and one guide whose address cannot be cited; it stays out.
The plot's age is given as planted in 1785, documented in 1850 and more than two hundred and fifty years; the record keeps more than two hundred years and the eighteenth century.

records.place: O Rosal, by the Miño, Rías Baixas, Galicia

wine.name: Terras Gauda O Rosal
wine.grapes: Albariño, about seven tenths, with Caíño Blanco and Loureira for the rest, their shares changing with the year.
wine.sites: Vineyards at O Rosal, near the mouth of the Miño by the Portuguese border; the subzone's rules ask for at least seven tenths Albariño and Loureira, with every grape grown in O Rosal.
wine.making: Picked by hand, each variety is kept apart, given a cold soak before fermentation whose length suits the grape, and fermented cool in stainless steel with native yeasts from the house's own vineyards. The three wines are then blended, cold stabilised, filtered and bottled young.
wine.glass: Pear, apple and ripe peach with grapefruit and a balsamic, minty lift over a stony, salty frame; rounder than a Salnés Albariño, with lively acidity and a fresh finish.
wine.ageing: Open and bright on release and at its freshest in the first two or three years, though its acidity carries it some years more.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; it needs no decanter; a white wine glass, beside octopus, clams or grilled sardines.

label.means: A Rías Baixas subzone by the Miño; a wine labelled with it holds at least seventy per cent Albariño and Loureira, all grown there.
The Denominación de Origen ratified in July 1988, with O Rosal among its three first subzones.

records.table: Terras Gauda O Rosal is a blend from the mouth of the Miño: mostly Albariño, with Loureira and Caíño Blanco, a rare grape the house set out to restore. Pear, apple and a minty lift; pour it cool beside octopus.
records.story: O Rosal lies in the south of Rías Baixas, where the Miño meets the Atlantic at the Portuguese border. When the Denominación de Origen was ratified in July 1988, O Rosal was one of its three first subzones, and its rules allow a blend: at least seventy per cent Albariño and Loureira, with other authorised grapes beside them, every one grown in the subzone. Terras Gauda was founded there by a Galician family at the turn of the 1990s, in 1989 by one account of its importer and 1990 by another. Its founders set out to restore Caíño Blanco, a white grape of the valley that had become rare, and made it a partner of Albariño and Loureira in their O Rosal. The house picks and ferments each variety apart, with yeasts from its own vineyards, and blends the three before bottling, so the wine shows the subzone rather than one grape. A label that names Albariño holds that grape alone; Terras Gauda O Rosal teaches the other legal path, a subzone blend, and a guest who asks why the bottle does not say Albariño should hear about Caíño Blanco.

others.note: The same three grapes of O Rosal, fermented in French oak and then aged on their lees.

traps: Terras Gauda O Rosal is a blend, not a varietal Albariño: a label naming the O Rosal subzone may hold Loureira, Caíño Blanco and other local grapes.
O Rosal blends Albariño with Loureira by the rules, while Condado do Tea pairs it with Treixadura; do not swap the two subzones' partners.

report: founded is left empty: the US importer's own pages give 1989 in one place and 1990 in another, the Rías Baixas promotion site gives 1989 and the Wine Scholar Guild guide 1990, so the story says the turn of the 1990s and names both years as the importer's.

The house's own domain gave no history or sheet, so the making rests on Bodeboca and Enterwine (hand picking, each variety apart, a cold soak, cool steel, native yeasts from its vineyards, blending, cold stabilising, filtering), with the importer for the native yeasts; the two to three months on the lees, given by the importer alone, is left out.
The blend's shares vary by vintage and by merchant (Albariño about seventy per cent each time, Caíño Blanco 18 to 25, Loureira 5 to 12), so the record gives about seven tenths and no more.

The O Rosal rule (at least seventy per cent Albariño and Loureira from the subzone) and the three first subzones of 1988 are the Consejo Regulador's own, from its wines page, its Pliego of 2012 and its history page.

Left out on one source each: the replanting of Caíño Blanco dated to 1989, the share of all Caíño Blanco in the region the house holds (80 or 98 per cent, and volatile), the name read as land of happiness, and the house's work of 2012 with the Spanish research council (CSIC) and the Misión Biológica de Galicia, which rests on Interempresas alone.
Living names met and kept out: the founding family's two children named by the importer (Antón and Carmen Fonseca), for the read-together agent; the founder is described, not named.
Searches for this record: 8 of the group's 35, one restricted to the house's domain and five to merchants', guides' and the importer's, with one more shared with Martín Códax.

changed: wine.sites, wine.label, story and cards: the O Rosal rule read as seventy per cent Albariño and Loureira grown in the subzone, with other local grapes; now seventy per cent Albariño and Loureira with other authorised grapes, every grape grown in O Rosal, as the regulating council's wines page and its rules of 2009 give it.

others: Etiqueta Negra was fermented and raised on its lees in French oak barrels; now fermented in French oak and then aged on its lees, since the house's sheet gives barrels and a merchant's sheet foudres and barrels by vintage.

sources: the Bodeboca sheet gives way to the house's own tasting notes for the 2023 vintage (about seven tenths Albariño, a cold soak whose length suits each variety, its own yeasts from its own vineyards, stabilised and bottled), a primary source for its own making.
open: founded stays empty: 1989 is the commoner year, with a first vintage in 1990, but a brand profile gives 1990 for the founding.
That each variety is fermented apart in steel rests on merchants (Enterwine, Bodeboca, Vinissimus); the house's sheet gives a cold soak by variety but does not say when the three are blended.

The replanting of Caíño Blanco dated to 1989 rests on one account and is not told; another producer outside O Rosal also worked to revive the grape, so the record says the house set out to restore it, never that it alone did.
